Hatchlings of the Australasian gannet (Morus serrator) emerge after an incubation period of 44 days [ab = 44 days] when maintained at 36 °C [T = 36 °C], a temperature slightly below the typical adult active body temperature. At this stage, the wet weight of the chick is approximately 91 grams [Wwb = approximately 91 grams], a modest initial mass that reflects the substantial yolk reserves required to fuel early development. This birth mass is notably low compared to the asymptotic weight of the nestling, which can reach up to 3500 grams [Wwi = up to 3500 grams] before fledging. The trajectory from a 91-gram hatchling to a near-adult-sized chick highlights the intense period of somatic growth that occurs under biparental provisioning. Adults of this species, by contrast, typically weigh around 2345 grams, indicating that nestlings often overshoot adult mass before undergoing a pre-fledging weight recession. This pattern of reaching a peak mass exceeding that of the adult is common among large seabirds and is thought to provide a buffer against periods of food scarcity during the critical transition to independence. The incubation temperature of 36 °C is within the typical range for sulids, though it can vary with environmental conditions and parental attendance patterns.

Under the thermal conditions typical of active metabolic periods in this species, which average 40.6 °C [T = 40.6 °C], a predictable sequence of developmental milestones occurs. Fledging, marked by the achievement of sustained flight, occurs at 108 days after hatching [tx = 108 days after hatching], a duration that aligns well with values reported for the congeneric northern gannet Morus bassanus at a temperature of 40.6 °C [T = 40.6 °C]. This extended nestling period allows for the complete development of flight feathers and the accumulation of sufficient lipid reserves to support the post-fledging dispersal phase. Following fledging, juvenile gannets experience a prolonged period of learning and self-feeding before they reach sexual maturity. The age at puberty, defined by the onset of gonadal activity, is estimated at 324 days after hatching [tp = 324 days after hatching] for this species at a temperature of 40.6 °C [T = 40.6 °C]. This value reflects the time required for young birds to achieve the physiological condition necessary for reproductive competence, though actual first breeding is typically deferred for several more years due to the constraints of territory acquisition and foraging skill development.

The age at first successful reproduction in Australasian gannets is deferred until approximately 730 days after hatching [tR = approximately 730 days after hatching], a delay that reflects the time needed to acquire a breeding territory and gain sufficient forag at a temperature of 40.6 °C [T = 40.6 °C]ing experience. This timing, recorded under the typical active body temperature of 40.6 °C, is broadly consistent with values documented for the closely related northern gannet Morus bassanus, which typically begins breeding at two to three years of age. The relatively late onset of reproduction is characteristic of long-lived seabirds with a slow life-history pace, where the benefits of delayed maturity are offset by increased adult survival and lifetime reproductive output. During the interval between achieving sexual maturity at 324 days and first breeding at 730 days, young gannets engage in prospecting behaviors, visiting colonies and establishing pair bonds. These pre-breeding years are critical for learning nest-site selection and developing the social skills necessary for successful reproduction, although mortality during this period is substantial due to inexperience and competition with established adults.

The maximum reproductive rate for Australasian gannets is constrained by their annual breeding cycle; females typically produce a single egg per clutch [N_R_i = single egg per clutch], and they raise one clutch per year [F_R_i = one clutch per year]. This low fecundity is characteristic of long-lived pelagic seabirds that invest heavily in each offspring. The incubation period of 44 days [ab = 44 days] at 36 °C represents a substantial energetic investment for the parents, who share incubation duties through a system of alternating shifts that can last for several days at a temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. Following hatching, the chick's rapid growth from its initial wet weight of 91 grams [Wwb = 91 grams] toward its asymptotic weight of 3500 grams [Wwi = 3500 grams] requires frequent provisioning trips by both parents. The reproductive output of this species is further constrained by the time required for the chick to reach fledging at 108 days after hatching [tx = 108 days after hatching], which occupies a significant portion of the annual cycle and precludes the possibility of multiple successful broods in a single year at a temperature of 40.6 °C [T = 40.6 °C].

Maximum lifespan in the Australasian gannet is estimated at 12045 days [am = 12045 days], which corresponds to approximately 33 years under the active body temperature of approximately 40.6 °C [T = 40.6 °C]. This longevity is within the range documented for other large sulids and is a key component of their life-history strategy, which prioritizes adult survival over high annual fecundity. The substantial investment in each offspring, from the 44-day incubation and the 108-day nestling period until fledging, combined with the subsequent delay until first reproduction at approximately 730 days after hatching, is only viable if adults can achieve a long reproductive lifespan. The trade-off between current reproduction and future survival is evident in the deferred age at first breeding, which allows young birds to develop the foraging skills necessary to provision offspring successfully. This slow life-history pace, together with the relatively late attainment of sexual maturity at around 324 days after hatching, positions the Australasian gannet as a classic K-selected species adapted to stable marine environments.
